claim: The fictional compiler opens by looking back to a simpler past when there was more time, folk were fewer and villages were proud and independent, so the record voice is itself retrospective.
source: Paul H. Kocher, Master of Middle-earth (1972), ch. VII
quote: villages were proud and independent still in those days

verdict.trueWording: he looks back to the happier past; villages proud and independent
verdict.note: Quote verbatim on the Wayback capture, and 'there was more time...and folk were fewer' is there too, as is the retrospective/nostalgic characterisation ('nostalgic about the greater simplicity of life in the old days of which he writes'). What Kocher never says is that this look-back OPENS the record; he places it nowhere in the text's order.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: that the nostalgic look-back is the compiler's opening ('opens by' / 'preamble') - Kocher never locates it at the start

claim: The tale closes with mock-learned derivations of Thame and Worminghall attributed to 'the learned in such matters', so place-name philology is the record's final word.
source: Tom Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth, ch. 4 'A Cartographic Plot'
quote: Thame with an h is a folly without warrant

verdict.trueWording: Tolkien ends by remarking... 'Thame with an h is a folly without warrant'
verdict.note: Retrieved from the Internet Archive full text (djvu.txt) of the item, pp. 90-91. Quote verbatim; 'ends by remarking' supports the closing position, and 'the whole story that Tolkien tells to account for the names of Thame and Worminghall is based on nothing, is mere fiction' supports the mock-learned derivations of both names. Shippey nowhere quotes or reports the in-tale attribution phrase.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: the attribution of the derivations to 'the learned in such matters' - that phrase appears nowhere in Shippey's text

claim: Farmer Giles carries a two-layer apparatus in one short foreword: an imagined editor faults an imagined author's geography, though that author 'lived himself in the lands of the Little Kingdom'.
source: Tom Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth, ch. 4 'A Cartographic Plot'
quote: the imagined 'editor' of Farmer Giles to criticise its imagined 'author'

verdict.trueWording: extremely unfair of the imagined 'editor'... to criticise its imagined 'author'
verdict.note: Quote verbatim, and the continuation is verbatim too: 'that "author", like Tolkien, "lived himself in the lands of the Little Kingdom" and knew what he was writing about.' The editor-over-author two-layer point is squarely Shippey's. What the page does not do is locate that apparatus in the Foreword or call it short; the word 'foreword' does not occur in the passage.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: that the two layers sit 'in one short foreword' - Shippey never names the Foreword or its length

claim: Distances and directions in the tale map onto real Oxfordshire places (Ham/Thame, Tamworth, Farthingho, the Rollright Stones) at a parochial scale, so the Little Kingdom is measured like a real county.
source: Tom Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth, ch. 4 'A Cartographic Plot'
quote: proof of the 'Little Kingdom's' lack of territorial ambition

verdict.trueWording: Thame in Buckinghamshire; Farthingho in Northamptonshire; parochial scale
verdict.note: Quote verbatim. Shippey gives Ham = now Thame, twelve miles east of Oxford; the Middle Kingdom's capital 'sounds like Tamworth... sixty-eight miles from Thame'; Farthingho 'on a direct line... about a third of the way' as 'proof of the Little Kingdom's lack of territorial ambition'; Wales and the Pennines 'on this parochial scale suitably far off'; the Standing Stones = the Rollright Stones on the Warwickshire/Oxfordshire boundary. The counties Shippey actually names are Buckinghamshire, Northamptonshire and Warwickshire, not Oxfordshire.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: 'real Oxfordshire places' - Shippey puts Thame in Buckinghamshire, Farthingho in Northamptonshire, and Tamworth as the Mercian capital

claim: The tale's narrator was 'Daddy' in the oral original, became 'the family jester', and took on a formal scholarly tone when the story was enlarged by half for an academic essay club in 1938.
source: Hammond & Scull, 'Farmer Giles of Ham' (Tolkien Estate)
quote: the family jester

verdict.unsupportedLimb: that the narrator took on a formal scholarly tone at the 1938 enlargement — the page dates the mock-scholarly voice to the 1949 revision instead
verdict.trueWording: For this larger, more academic audience, he added many proper names, jokes, and allusions
verdict.note: Raw page fetched (200, live). Quote 'the family jester' is verbatim: 'In the second version of the story, the narrator is "the family jester"'. Supported: narrated by 'Daddy' in the first version; 'enlarging it by some fifty per cent' in January 1938 for the Lovelace Society, 'an undergraduate essay club at Oxford's Worcester College'. NOT supported: any narratorial shift to scholarly tone at that 1938 stage — the page says the 1938 additions were 'proper names, jokes, and allusions', and places the apparatus later: 'Tolkien again revised the text, and added a mock foreword' before the 1949 publication. Second minor slip: 'Daddy' narrates the first written version, not the oral original.

claim: The Prologue says 'pipe-weed' rather than tobacco because the imported word would sound wrong, and hedges its botany with a Latin binomial instead.
source: Tom Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth
quote: a variety probably of Nicotiana

verdict.unsupportedLimb: 'a Latin binomial' — the page shows only the genus name, Tolkien's hedge 'a variety probably of Nicotiana', which is a uninomial, not a binomial
verdict.trueWording: Why not say 'tobacco', since the plant is 'a variety probably of Nicotiana'? Because the word would sound wrong
verdict.note: Same raw book text, ch. 3 'The Bourgeois Burglar', around the p. 63-64 running heads. Quote 'a variety probably of Nicotiana' verbatim, and the pipe-weed-not-tobacco reason is verbatim ('Because the word would sound wrong ... It is an import from some unknown Caribbean language via Spanish'). The only defective limb is the botanical label: a binomial needs genus plus species, and neither Shippey nor the Prologue supplies one.

claim: The Prologue is a richly textured anthropology of the hobbits, delivered in an editorial voice of scholarly distance, and notes that hobbits liked books that set out what they already knew fair and square with no contradictions.
source: Thomas J. West III, 'Tolkien Tuesdays: Re-Reading The Lord of the Rings: Prologue'
quote: a richly-textured anthropology about the hobbits

verdict.trueWording: a richly-textured anthropology about the hobbits and the Shire
verdict.note: omnivorous.substack.com raw HTML carries the full post. Quote verbatim: 'a richly-textured anthropology about the hobbits and the Shire that they call home'. The books limb is verbatim too: 'they liked to have books filled with things that they already knew, set out fair and square with no contradictions' (7). But nothing on the page describes the Prologue's voice as editorial or scholarly or as keeping distance — the only tonal characterisations are 'more light-hearted than heavy' and 'It's not condescending, exactly'; the words scholarly, editorial, academic and detached do not occur, and the single hit for 'distance' is the hobbits distancing themselves from the Elves.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: delivered in an editorial voice of scholarly distance

claim: Every stage of the Red Book's fictional transmission carries two datings, an Age-date and a Shire-reckoning equivalent, so the records cross-reference two calendars.
source: Alexander Schmitt, 'Stages and Logic of the fictitious tradition of Tolkien's Legendarium' (schematax.org, 2021)

verdict.note: schematax PDF fetched raw (HTTP 200, 3 pp.). The quote 'IV 172 / S.R. 1592' is verbatim, at stages (13), (14), (15) and in the timeline, and dual Age/Shire dating is indeed the schema's pervasive habit: (2) III 3002 / S.R. 1402, (3) III 3003-3018 / S.R. 1403-1418, (8) IV 62 / S.R. 1482, (11) IV 64 / S.R. 1484, and so on. But 'every stage' is falsified by the same page: stage (1) 'Bilbo has diaries containing his recountings of his quest for Erebor' carries no date at all, and stage (7) is printed as '(7) ? Sam makes his additions.' Two of the fifteen stages carry no dating, so the universal quantifier fails on the page that is cited for it.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: every stage ... carries two datings (stages (1) and (7) carry none)

claim: Appendix A's Kings of the Mark section uses annalistic headings, dates recording great events, and later editor's footnotes (such as identifying Holdwine as Meriadoc), giving the look of authentic historical documentation.
source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's frame stories'

verdict.trueWording: the Holdwine=Meriadoc identification is labelled 'Scribal gloss', not 'Later editor's footnote'
verdict.unsupportedLimb: the parenthetical example - the page assigns 'Later editor's footnote' to the footnote about Eowyn's shield-arm, and labels the bracketed '[This Holdwine was none other than Meriadoc the Magnificent who was Master of Buckland.]' a 'Scribal gloss', a distinct third category
verdict.note: § Paratexts table (Croft 2018) supports the rest: the row labels are 'Annalistic heading', 'Annalistic dates and text recording great events of the past', 'Later editor's footnote' and 'Scribal gloss', over Appendix A. II 'The House of Eorl', The Kings of the Mark, Third Line. The 'look of authentic historical documentation' limb is supported in other words - the paratexts 'resonat[e]' or 'collaborat[e]' with the main text 'making it more believable', under the table caption 'Tolkien's representation of historical editing of ancient documents'. The claim's quote field is empty, so the grade turns wholly on the limbs.

claim: Turner notes the frame works at two levels at once, treating the world of the story as historical fact while creating for the reader the illusion of a direct link through time and space.
source: Wikipedia, 'Editorial framing of The Lord of the Rings' (citing Turner)
quote: the world of the story as historical fact

verdict.trueWording: elements of the frame story function at multiple levels
verdict.unsupportedLimb: the count 'two levels at once' - the page (and its section heading) says 'multiple levels', never two
verdict.note: § Multiple levels: "The scholar of literature Allan Turner comments that elements of the frame story function at multiple levels; in particular, metatextual elements like the appendices '[treat] the world of the story as historical fact, at the same time [creating] for the reader the illusion of a direct link through time and space with his/her own world through the persona of the \"editor\"'." The quote is verbatim and the two substantive halves (historical fact; illusion of a direct link through time and space) are both supported; only the numeral is the page's 'multiple', and the claim also drops the closing qualifier 'with his/her own world through the persona of the editor'.

claim: The translator persona of Appendix F would rather change the English language and coin new words than deliver a substandard translation, so consistency of rendering governs the whole record.
source: N. Lurquin, 'Translating the Red Book of Westmarch' (Tolkien: Medieval and Modern blog)
quote: rather change the English language and make new words

verdict.trueWording: his forward in the first edition of The Fellowship of the Ring
verdict.unsupportedLimb: 'the translator persona of Appendix F' - the post grounds the translator conceit in Tolkien's foreword to the first edition of The Fellowship of the Ring and never mentions Appendix F (zero occurrences on the page)
verdict.note: Live blogspot page, HTTP 200. The quoted limb is verbatim: 'He would rather change the English language and make new words than provide us with a substandard translation.' The consistency limb is supported in other words: 'He created words in the English language simply so he could consistently translate the Red Book of Westmarch from Westron into English.' Only the Appendix F locus fails; the post's stated source is 'his forward in the first edition of The Fellowship of the Ring'.

feature: annals versus Tales as two modes
claim: Tolkien told Waldman that the Rings of Power and the Downfall of Númenor were dealt with annalistically and in two Tales or Accounts, naming a two-mode scheme of compressed annal and expanded tale.
source: Norbert Schürer, 'Second Age, Middle Age', JTR 15.2 (2022), quoting Letter 131
quote: dealt with annalistically, and in two Tales or Accounts

verdict.trueWording: Tolkien: "dealt with annalistically, and in two Tales or Accounts" (Letters 151)
verdict.note: Raw PDF reached via Wayback (live viewcontent.cgi 403s). Quote verbatim on PDF sheet 10 = article p. 8: 'Tolkien writes that The Rings of Power and the Downfall of Numenor are "dealt with annalistically, and in two Tales or Accounts" (Letters 151)'. Schuerer does NOT read this as two modes: he says 'These tales or accounts are perhaps the annals collected in the section "The Tale of Years of the Second Age"', i.e. he identifies the tales WITH the annals rather than opposing compressed annal to expanded tale.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: naming a two-mode scheme of compressed annal and expanded tale

claim: Tolkien's annals are modelled on the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, with entries opening 'Here' or 'In this year', and his Old English versions use the early West Saxon dialect of the Chronicle's earliest parts.
source: Himring, 'Fingon's rescue of Maedhros in Old English' (Silmarillion Writers' Guild)
quote: early West Saxon (second half of the ninth century)

verdict.trueWording: annals clearly inspired by Anglo-Saxon Chronicle; dialect early West Saxon
verdict.note: Quote verbatim: 'The dialect of these annals is the early West Saxon (second half of the ninth century) of traditional Old English textbooks and of the earliest parts of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle'; also 'The style of Tolkien's annals ... is clearly inspired by the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle'. The opening-formula limb is only shown by one example, never stated as a convention: the AB I year-2 entry reads 'Here Fingon son of Fingolfin healed the feud...' / OE 'Her Fingon Fingolfines sunu...' cribbed as 'Here (this year)'. The page never writes 'In this year', and the other displayed entry opens 'Tha weartd' ('Then was').
verdict.unsupportedLimb: that annal entries open 'Here' or 'In this year' as a convention

claim: Barkley argues the main part of the Tale is narrated by Aragorn and Armstrong considers Arwen as narrator after his death, so the annal admits embedded first-person witnesses within an editorial frame.
source: Wikipedia, 'The Tale of Aragorn and Arwen'
quote: narrated by Aragorn

verdict.trueWording: considers the main part narrated by Aragorn; Armstrong: Arwen narrator
verdict.note: Both attributions verbatim: Barkley 'considers the main part of the tale to have been narrated by Aragorn'; footnote: Armstrong 'examines the implications of one of the narrators of the tale being Arwen as she related the story after Aragorn's death'. The page frames this as narrative voice / point of view and never says the narration is first-person, nor calls the text an annal; the editorial frame is real (Pezzini's 'scribal glosses, later notes, and editorial references') but the synthesis limb is the claimant's, not the page's.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: so the annal admits embedded first-person witnesses within an editorial frame

claim: Appendix A reads like a real history because its narrative style is that of a historian summarising primary documents rather than a novelist.
source: Tolkien Geek, 'Appendix A (Part One)'
quote: reads like a real history

verdict.trueWording: Appendix A reads like a real history; historian summarizing primary documents
verdict.note: Live page reached. Sentence: 'Appendix A reads like a real history and Tolkien's narrative style is that of an historian who is summarizing information that he derived from primary documents.' Quote verbatim and the historian/primary-documents limb verbatim, but the post 'novel'/'novelist' contrast does not appear anywhere on the page (the only hit for 'author' is a commenter), and the page joins the two clauses with 'and', not a causal 'because'.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: rather than a novelist (the page never contrasts historian with novelist)

claim: Shippey reports Tolkien's working rule that one should always start with a name, because a name produces a story, which underlies the place-name etymologies that open and close his civic records.
source: Tom Shippey, 'J.R.R. Tolkien and Philology' (Tolkien Estate)
quote: Give me a name and it produces a story

verdict.trueWording: I always in writing, always start with a name
verdict.note: Live page reached. Quote verbatim as a pull-quote: 'I always in writing, always start with a name. Give me a name and it produces a story.' - but the page credits it to 'Tolkien, audio interview by Denys Gueroult, 1965', not to Shippey's reporting; Shippey's own prose says only that names are the widest 'survivor-genre', 'full of buried information', and that Tolkien 'took deep personal interest in names, and was always ready to consider their etymologies'. The application limb is absent from the page entirely.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: which underlies the place-name etymologies that open and close his civic records

claim: Raffel grants The Lord of the Rings magnificence but denies it the status of literature, on grounds including style.
source: Burton Raffel 1968, p. 218, as quoted in Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist, Introduction n. 11
quote: is not literature

verdict.trueWording: We disagree with critics like Burton Raffel who declares that while 'The Lord of the Rings is a magnificent performance, full of charm, excitement, and affection [...] it is not [...] literature' (Raffel 218)
verdict.note: Raw page reached only through a real browser (curl and WebFetch both hit Springer's JS 'Client Challenge'; no Wayback capture exists; Crossref and OpenAlex carry no abstract). Note 11 is exactly as above, so magnificence-granted and literature-denied are both supported and the p.218 cite matches the Works Cited entry (Raffel, 'The Lord of the Rings as Literature', 1968, 218-246). Two defects: the quoted words are not contiguous on the page - the page reads 'it is not [...] literature' with a bracketed elision, not 'is not literature' - and the note gives no reason at all for Raffel's verdict.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: 'on grounds including style' - note 11 states Raffel's verdict without giving any grounds, stylistic or otherwise

claim: Siepmann characterises Kirk's 1971 essay as praise of Tolkien's ordinary yet dignified diction, against Wilson's scorn.
source: Elizabeth Kirk 1971 (1977 reprint), as characterised in Siepmann CL2017
quote: Tolkien's ordinary yet dignified diction

verdict.trueWording: praise of Tolkien's ordinary yet dignified diction (Kirk, 1977, Rosebury, 2003, p. 22)
verdict.note: Quote verbatim in the PDF's opening sentence, and the against-Wilson framing is supported by the 'ranging from scathing criticisms... to praise of...' construction. But the page dates Kirk 1977, not 1971, in both the in-text citation and the reference list: 'Kirk, E. (1977). I Would Rather Have Written in Elvish: Language, Fiction, and The Lord of the Rings. Novel 5, 5-18. Reprinted in M. Spilka (Ed.) (1977) Towards a Poetics of Fiction'. The year 1971 appears nowhere in the paper.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: 'Kirk's 1971 essay' - the page dates the essay 1977 in both citation and reference list, and never prints 1971

claim: The book marks the unashamed return of gorgeous, eloquent heroic romance in an anti-romantic age.
source: Lewis 1954
quote: heroic romance, gorgeous, eloquent, and unashamed

verdict.trueWording: "it makes not a return but an advance or revolution"
verdict.unsupportedLimb: that the book 'marks the return' of heroic romance — Lewis calls exactly that formulation 'inadequate' and says that in the history of Romance itself it is 'not a return but an advance or revolution: the conquest of new territory'
verdict.note: Quote 'heroic romance, gorgeous, eloquent, and unashamed' is verbatim, inside the sentence 'To say that in it heroic romance, gorgeous, eloquent, and unashamed, has suddenly returned at a period almost pathological in its anti-romanticism, is inadequate.' The anti-romantic-age limb is supported; the unqualified 'return' limb is the one Lewis explicitly overrides (he concedes only that 'To us, who live in that odd period, the return and the sheer relief of it is doubtless the important thing').

claim: Olsen's close reading tracks changes in tone as The Hobbit's stakes grow and distinguishes High Elves from Mirkwood elves through their speech.
source: David Oberhelman, Mythopoeic Society review of Corey Olsen, Exploring J.R.R. Tolkien's The Hobbit
quote: changes in tone as the stakes become greater

verdict.trueWording: "His discussion of the 'silly' singing elves of Rivendell highlights the differences"
verdict.unsupportedLimb: that Olsen distinguishes High Elves from Mirkwood elves 'through their speech' — Oberhelman attributes the contrast to Olsen's discussion of the singing elves of Rivendell and to close readings of the songs, and never says the two kinds are told apart by speech
verdict.note: First limb verbatim: Olsen 'traces certain themes such as Bilbo's choices, luck and providence in his adventures, and the changes in tone as the stakes become greater throughout the course of the novel.' Second limb's substance is adjacent — 'His discussion of the "silly" singing elves of Rivendell highlights the differences between these High Elves and the lower ones of Mirkwood' — but the page grounds it in song and in Olsen's discussion, not in a speech contrast between the two groups.

claim: Mythgard's Exploring The Lord of the Rings is an explicitly sentence-level reading, but no transcripts or notes are published; only titles are public.
source: Mythgard Institute, Exploring the Lord of the Rings project page
quote: sentence by sentence

verdict.trueWording: “we read through a portion of the text, sentence by sentence”
verdict.unsupportedLimb: no transcripts or notes are published; only titles are public
verdict.note: Raw HTML fetched (curl, browser UA, HTTP 200, 65,817 B) and tag-stripped: the quote is verbatim in the 'Deep Reading and Commentary' block. The page never uses the word 'transcript' (grep -ic transcript = 0) and says nothing about notes or about only titles being public; on the contrary it advertises 'All episodes are recorded and added to the Signum University YouTube channel' plus a podcast feed, Twitch livestreams, Discord and a discussion forum, so the second limb is unsupported and in tension with the page.

claim: The instinct of linguistic invention is the fitting of notion to oral symbol and pleasure in contemplating the relation — words must sound like what they mean.
source: Tolkien, 'A Secret Vice' (full text, gwern PDF)
quote: the fitting of notion to oral symbol

verdict.trueWording: “the fitting of notion to oral symbol, and pleasure in contemplating the new relation”
verdict.unsupportedLimb: words must sound like what they mean
verdict.note: PDF downloaded from gwern (HTTP 200, 957,151 B, 26 pp — the 'A Secret Vice' text as printed in The Monsters and the Critics) and text-extracted with pdfminer. Quote verbatim: 'The instinct for “linguistic invention” - the fitting of notion to oral symbol, and pleasure in contemplating the new relation established, is rational, and not perverted.' The essay locates the pleasure in the contemplated RELATION between sound and notion — 'it is the contemplation of the relation between sound and notion which is a main source of pleasure', 'a private sense of fitness', 'word-form in relation to meaning (so-called phonetic fitness)' — an invented, personal fitness, not mimicry. Nowhere does the page prescribe that words must sound like what they mean; that limb is the claim's own gloss.

claim: An invented language with individual flavour must have a mythology woven into it, and conversely language construction will breed a mythology — names and tongue come first, the world grows to fit.
source: Tolkien, 'A Secret Vice'
quote: your language construction will breed a mythology

verdict.trueWording: your language construction will breed a mythology
verdict.note: Quote verbatim. Limbs 1-2 fully supported: 'to give your language an individual flavour, it must have woven into it the threads of an individual mythology' and 'The converse indeed is true, your language construction will breed a mythology.' The third limb is not on this page: 'A Secret Vice' nowhere says names come first or that a world grows to fit them. Greps for names/world/stories return only unrelated passages (Animalic animal names, Welsh names on coal-trucks, 'history of the world'). The names-first/world-to-fit formulation is Letters #165/#180, not this essay. Language->mythology priority IS supported; names and world are not.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: names and tongue come first, the world grows to fit

claim: Linguistic taste is partly inborn (the 'native tongue' as distinct from the cradle-tongue), so a writer's phonaesthetic choices express inherent predilections rather than fashion.
source: Anna Smol, 'Tolkien's cellar door' (quoting 'English and Welsh' pp.190-1)
quote: inherent linguistic predilections

verdict.trueWording: Tolkien discusses our 'inherent linguistic predilections' (p. 190)
verdict.note: Quote 'inherent linguistic predilections' is verbatim, with the claimed p.190 citation, and the page supplies the p.191 cellar-door passage — so the pp.190-1 source line is right. But the page never mentions a native tongue or a cradle-tongue: greps for 'cradle', 'native tongue' and bare 'native' return zero hits, and 'fashion' returns zero. The page's support for inbornness is only 'inherent linguistic predilections' plus 'everyone has a preference for certain sounds dissociated from the meanings of words'. The native/cradle-tongue distinction is genuinely in 'English and Welsh', but it is NOT on this cited page.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: the 'native tongue' as distinct from the cradle-tongue (and 'rather than fashion')

claim: The language should be intentionally antiquated but not arcane — words still in literary use among educated people — avoiding both the colloquial and the obscure.
source: Philip Irving Mitchell (DBU), outline of 'On Translating Beowulf'
quote: avoid both the colloquial and the obscure

verdict.trueWording: antiquated not arcane; avoid the colloquial and the obscure
verdict.unsupportedLimb: 'words still in literary use among educated people' — that qualifier appears nowhere on the DBU page (full page text read, 6,116 chars; no occurrence of 'educated' or 'literary use')
verdict.note: Raw dbu.edu page fetched by curl (200). Quote 'avoid both the colloquial and the obscure' is verbatim, and 'intentionally antiquated but not intentionally arcane' supports that limb; the 'still in literary use among educated people' gloss is imported from Tolkien's essay, not from this page.

claim: Resolving Old English compounds into phrases keeps colour but loosens and weakens the texture; compact naming is preferred.
source: Wikipedia, 'On Translating Beowulf'
quote: loosens and weakens the texture

verdict.trueWording: 'Choice between the evils will vary with occasions'
verdict.unsupportedLimb: 'compact naming is preferred' — the page states no preference; it says the naming method 'retains the compactness of the original but loses its colour' and closes 'Choice between the evils will vary with occasions'
verdict.note: Raw Wikipedia page fetched by curl (200). Quote 'loosens and weakens the texture' verbatim, and the colour/texture trade-off is exactly as claimed; but the page presents the two methods as balanced evils rather than favouring compact naming.

claim: Intelligent children of good taste single out the points in manner where the address is to children as blemishes.
source: Tolkien Gateway, 'Letter 215'
quote: singled out the places where the address was to children

source: Tolkien Gateway, 'Letter 194'

verdict.trueWording: a tale told epically

source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style' (quoting Appendix F)
quote: quick to note and adopt the style
